statement: Some medicines, their breakdown products and a few foods and other products have been reported to make particular urine drug screens read positive when the drug screened for was absent, as described second-hand in two narrative reviews: a review by laboratory-medicine authors of reports published from 2000 on, with a stated search that found 173 articles, 62 of them with data on false positives (Saitman et al., 2014), and a clinical review for clinicians (Moeller et al., 2017). Screens are immunoassays: they use antibodies, which can also bind other substances, including ones whose structure looks unlike the target, and breakdown products. Each report concerns particular tests, and the same medicine often left other tests unaffected; most reports are single case reports, reviews of patients' charts, or experiments adding a medicine to drug-free urine, and some concern tests that have since changed. Examples with counts: in a blinded study, one point-of-care benzodiazepine test was positive in 46 of 50 people taking the HIV medicine efavirenz and negative in 47 of 50 not taking it, while two other point-of-care tests and LC-MS/MS were negative on all the positives; efavirenz also gave false-positive cannabis screens through a breakdown product on three immunoassays, and in another study one brand of test strips was positive in 28 of 30 people taking it while another device and two laboratory assays were negative; and one laboratory amphetamine assay was negative in 6 healthy men before two doses of the antibiotic ofloxacin and positive in all 6 after. By screen, the reviews name, among others: for amphetamine screens, which the clinical review calls the screens most often linked to false positives, pseudoephedrine and ephedrine, bupropion, labetalol, ranitidine, metformin, the supplement DMAA and trazodone (through its breakdown product, on one ecstasy screen and one amphetamine screen but not another), in a table of 33 entries (among them phentermine, methylphenidate and atomoxetine) that mixes false positives with true ones such as prescribed dextroamphetamine and names no tests or frequencies; for benzodiazepine screens, sertraline, efavirenz and oxaprozin; for cannabis screens, efavirenz, NSAID painkillers (2 false positives in 510 samples in one study, called rare), proton pump inhibitors (one case report and a package insert) and, in newborns' urine, several baby wash products at a 20 ng/mL cutoff; for opiate screens, quinolone antibiotics, rifampicin, naloxone added to urine at high concentrations, and poppy seeds (the US federal workplace cutoff for morphine was raised from 300 to 2,000 ng/mL in 1998 to limit positives from poppy seeds and prescribed opiates); for PCP screens, venlafaxine, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine and tramadol (in case reports, after overdose), the laboratory review adding that a positive PCP screen is rarely a true positive because PCP use is rare and the tests are not specific; for methadone screens, quetiapine, verapamil, diphenhydramine and doxylamine; and for buprenorphine screens, morphine and other opioids added to urine, so that heroin use could make a buprenorphine screen read positive. Only a few frequencies are printed, and none is the chance that a person taking a medicine will screen positive: in one chart review, 41% of amphetamine screens that GC-MS did not confirm (53 patients; the total is not printed) came from people taking bupropion, with no experiment showing that bupropion caused it; in another, 26.5% of benzodiazepine screens that confirmation did not support (26 samples) were linked to sertraline, again without such an experiment (the clinical review gives 27% to 32% from two chart reviews without saying of what); and in a US Department of Defense analysis the supplement DMAA was found in 92.3% of false-positive amphetamine samples. Some medicines give true positives because they are, or turn into, the substance tested for: prescribed amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine on amphetamine screens; dronabinol, a prescribed form of THC, on cannabis screens, which confirmation cannot tell from cannabis; and codeine, which the body turns partly into morphine. Cocaine screens cross-react little: the clinical review finds no evidence for the claim that amoxicillin makes them positive (four immunoassays tested showed none) and says that numbing medicines such as lidocaine, benzocaine, procaine and tetracaine do not, whereas cocaine used as a medical anaesthetic gives true positives and coca leaf tea can make cocaine screens positive. Alcohol tests for ethyl glucuronide can turn positive after hand sanitizer or mouthwash. Both reviews say a screen is presumptive and should be confirmed by a different method, such as GC-MS or LC-MS/MS, which identifies the substance: the clinical review advises always confirming before legal, employment or other decisions with serious consequences, and the laboratory review notes that such testing is limited or absent in many hospital laboratories and takes days, so decisions are often made on unconfirmed screens. The reviews disagree on one test: the clinical review says efavirenz affects the Drug Screen Multi 5 benzodiazepine test, citing the blinded study and another, while the laboratory review reports that test as negative on the efavirenz positives in the blinded study. The laboratory review also says, without data, that in most cases the cause of a false-positive screen is unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can medicines cause a false positive on a drug test? Yes, some can, on particular tests, according to two expert reviews, which are not new studies. Quick urine screens use antibodies that can react to look-alike molecules. On one benzodiazepine test, 46 of 50 people taking the HIV medicine efavirenz screened positive, although a different lab method found no benzodiazepine and two other quick tests stayed negative. The reviews list, among others, sertraline on benzodiazepine screens; bupropion, pseudoephedrine, labetalol and some others on amphetamine screens; some antibiotics on opiate screens; and venlafaxine, dextromethorphan and tramadol on PCP screens. Most of these come from single case reports or lab experiments with one test. Only a few rough figures exist, and none says how often people taking a medicine screen positive: in one review of patients' charts, 41 in 100 amphetamine screens that a second method did not confirm came from people taking bupropion; in another, about 27 in 100 false benzodiazepine screens were linked to sertraline. Some medicines give true positives because they are, or become, the drug tested for, such as prescribed amphetamines, prescribed THC (dronabinol) and codeine, which the body partly turns into morphine. There is no evidence that amoxicillin makes cocaine tests positive, and numbing medicines such as lidocaine do not. Both reviews say a screen should be checked by a different lab method before decisions with serious consequences.
population: People whose urine was screened for drugs while taking medicines, or after eating or using products, that might react with the screen, as described second-hand in two narrative reviews of published case reports, chart reviews and dosing studies, and of laboratory experiments adding medicines to drug-free urine (reports published from 2000 on in one review; literature from 1946 to 2016 in the other)
exposure: Medicines and their breakdown products (among them efavirenz, sertraline, bupropion, labetalol, pseudoephedrine, trazodone, quinolone antibiotics, rifampicin, venlafaxine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, quetiapine and NSAIDs), a supplement (DMAA), foods (poppy seeds, coca leaf tea) and products (baby wash, hand sanitizer, mouthwash) in urine tested with named screening immunoassays
comparator: Confirmation by a different method (GC-MS, LC-MS/MS or another chromatographic method) showing the target drug absent; drug-free urine before a medicine was added; urine before dosing; in one blinded study, people not taking the medicine
outcome: False-positive screening results (a positive immunoassay screen without the target drug) on named tests, the concentration at which they occurred where tested, and how often, where printed; true positives from medicines that are, or become, the substance tested for
magnitude: Saitman et al. (2014), as described: efavirenz, Biosite Triage 8 benzodiazepine test, blinded, 46 of 50 taking efavirenz positive and 47 of 50 not taking it negative; Drug Control 008, Drug Screen Multi 5 and LC-MS/MS negative on all presumptive positives; efavirenz, Rapid Response cannabis test strips positive in 28 of 30 people taking it for at least 2 weeks, the other point-of-care device and two automated assays negative; ofloxacin, one amphetamine assay (Abbott TDxFLx), 0 of 6 samples positive before and 6 of 6 after two doses in healthy men, the lowest almost four times the 300 ng/mL cutoff; promethazine and chlorpromazine, 3 and 6 specimens positive on Syva EMIT-MAM and negative by LC-PDA, all 9 negative on Syva EMIT-A and Biosite Triage, 2 positive on Agilent TesTcard 9; bupropion, 41% (53 patients) of Syva EMIT II Plus amphetamine positives not confirmed by GC-MS, total not printed (about 129 if 53 is 41%, editors' arithmetic), no spiking; sertraline, 26.5% (26 samples) of benzodiazepine screens positive on the Abbott Architect and Aeroset and negative on confirmation, January 2007 to December 2008, no spiking (about 98 false positives in all if 26 is 26.5%, editors' arithmetic); niflumic acid, 55 of 55 samples from 5 volunteers positive on Roche KIMS THC and negative on Syva EMIT; ambroxol, unexpected positive LSD screens (CEDIA) in twelve patients; buprenorphine screen (CEDIA, 5 ng/mL) and tramadol, false positives removed by a 20 ng/mL cutoff. Moeller et al. (2017), as described: sertraline and benzodiazepine screens, 27% to 32% in two retrospective studies, denominators not stated; NSAIDs and cannabis screens, 2 false positives in 510 samples (one with ibuprofen, one with naproxen; Saitman et al. list the same study's ibuprofen and naproxen results as case reports); PCP screens, false-positive rates of 24% with dextromethorphan, 22% with tramadol and 15% with diphenhydramine in urines not confirmed by GC-MS, denominators not stated; DMAA in 92.3% of false-positive amphetamine samples confirmed negative by GC-MS (US Department of Defense analysis); amoxicillin, no false-positive cocaine results on 4 immunoassays; federal opiate (morphine) screening cutoff raised from 300 to 2,000 ng/mL in 1998; Table 4, 33 entries for amphetamine screens (editors' count), mixing true and false positives, with no tests, concentrations or frequencies.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Materials and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Review of false-positive interferences with urine drug-screen immunoassays by laboratory-medicine authors (University of California, San Diego; Samsung Medical Center, Seoul). SciFinder (MEDLINE and CAPLUS) was searched with 'false positive [drug] urine' for amphetamines, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, cannabinoids and opiates, a miscellaneous class and over 60 common medicines and illicit drugs, in English, for articles published after 2000: 173 articles, of which 62 held data on false-positive results; older articles were used to clarify. False negatives are not covered. The authors rank evidence from weakest (exposure to the suspected medicine stated, or two-dimensional structures compared) to stronger (a pure standard added at several concentrations to drug-free urine), with chart reviews and measurement in patients' specimens as supportive, and dosing studies with confirmation also used. The introduction says mass-spectrometry testing is limited or absent in many hospital laboratories and its results usually take several days, so care decisions are often made on presumptive positives; that patients with false positives may lose eligibility in rehabilitation programmes or their jobs; and, without data, that in most cases the cause of a false-positive screen is unknown.

evidence.extracted: All immunoassay results are considered presumptive until confirmed by an independent chemical technique such as GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Antibodies bind three-dimensional structures, so compounds whose two-dimensional structures look unlike the target, and metabolites, can cause false positives; adding only the parent drug to drug-free urine without a positive result does not rule a medicine out.

risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through two narrative reviews (cards sc_saitman_2014: some concerns; sc_moeller_2017: high). The laboratory review states its search but used one string per drug on one platform, without duplicate screening, and a search for 'false positive' finds reports of interference rather than of tests that did not react; the clinical review's selection is unsystematic, and its Table 4 mixes true and false positives without tests, concentrations or frequencies. The reports themselves are mostly single case reports, chart reviews without experiments (bupropion, sertraline) and spiking experiments.

inconsistency.note: Where the same medicine was tested on several assays, results differed by assay, which the statement gives as the rule rather than a contradiction; the reviews disagree on one test (efavirenz and the Drug Screen Multi 5), which the statement reports.

indirectness.note: Second-hand. Each interference applies to the named test, and some tests have since changed (the clinical review notes that newer amphetamine assays no longer react to the Vicks inhaler); spiking experiments used concentrations not shown to occur in people's urine; the printed frequencies are shares of unconfirmed positives, not the chance that a person taking the medicine will screen positive.

imprecision.note: The few frequencies come from single chart reviews of 26 to 53 linked results with their totals unprinted, from groups of 6, 30 or 50 people, or from percentages without denominators.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; that reports of interference are likelier to be published than reports of none is counted under risk of bias.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: Reports of false-positive screens are case reports, chart reviews, small dosing studies and laboratory experiments, seen here only through two narrative reviews: they start low (METHODS §6.3: claims seen only through reviews start from the design of the primary studies and are rated down for risk of bias and indirectness); risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 take the claim to very low, the floor. It rests only on narrative reviews, so it stays at draft and says that its figures are second-hand. The rule for test accuracy (METHODS §6.3) was considered and not applied: the claim says which medicines were reported to cause false positives on which tests, not how often a test reads right; the one accuracy-type comparison, efavirenz on one benzodiazepine test in 100 people with LC-MS/MS as the reference, is seen second-hand. Status replicated: separate reports by different teams, described in both reviews, agree that particular medicines can make particular screens read positive when confirmation finds no drug (efavirenz on cannabis screens in two studies, quinolone antibiotics on opiate screens in several); most single medicine-and-test pairs rest on one report, and the two reviews share sources, counted once. Nothing is phrased as advice on avoiding or passing a test; the clinical review's section on tampering with samples was not used.
